title_original: Posterized November 2026: Bitter Christmas, Club Kid, Mouse & More
excerpt_original: The Hunger Games. Rocky Balboa. Godzilla. Ebenezer Scrooge. Cliff Booth? November is chock full of IP hoping to secure massive Thanksgiving holiday receipts at the box office, but don’t let those familiar names shield your attention from the buzzy indies and Oscar hopefuls…

blocks.text: The Hunger Games. Rocky Balboa. Godzilla. Ebenezer Scrooge. Cliff Booth?

November is chock full of IP hoping to secure massive Thanksgiving holiday receipts at the box office, but don’t let those familiar names shield your attention from the buzzy indies and Oscar hopefuls screening beside them.

This is the first big drop of award season goodies vying for any leg up they can muster as far as piquing Academy members’ interest. So, your ticket purchase means a lot more for the festival darlings than it does the board of directors of whichever shareholder-driven CEO is currently holding an Infinity Gauntlet of legacy studio cachet.
Maybe some of the below posters will sway you.
Together

Brandon Schaefer and Jump Cut start things off with the simple yet effective one-sheet for Soul Patrol (limited, November 6). It utilizes a great candid shot of the film’s subject: the Vietnam War’s first Black special ops team. The muted colors and grainy texture put the era on display while the demeanor of these men provides a promise for inspiration rather than tragedy.

From there the text falls in on the center y-axis to keep our eyes moving up and down vertically from laurels to quotes to titles to image and back again. The pop of red with the title isn’t overpowering thanks to a gradient fade into the gray sky and the unassuming sans serif of the whole ensures the men always remain our focus.

Did I sneak in a little IP next courtesy of AV Print’s Focker-in-Law (November 25)? Yes, but it’s a fun concept that keeps the ethos of the series alive without the need of any crazy swings. All that’s necessary is a quick shift of the frame.

Not only is cropping Ben Stiller out of the picture hilarious on its own, but it’s even funnier to see that he’s the only one trying to be in the photo in the first place. His one eye is looking directly at us while De Niro side-eyes Stiller and Grande side-eyes De Niro. It’s all about the franchise’s themes of mistrust and skepticism. Rather than tease that Greg might become Jack where his new future daughter-in-law is concerned, however, should we wonder if she’s the one judging whether the Fockers are worthy of her?
That ambiguity is what makes it noteworthy. The other layout with a lie detector scene? That just makes it seem like they’ve remade the first film.

From a group to a trio, we now move to a kinetic pair dancing in a bright, kaleidoscopic radial blur courtesy of George McWilliams (for GrandSon with photography by Ryan McGinley). Instead of just putting another glossy image on the wall, they deliver Club Kid (limited, November 6; wide, November 25) with a textured atmosphere that seeks to depict the scene’s energy more than its environment.

That’s why they push the text to the bottom. They don’t want to risk boxing in the rainbow of colors any more than the edges of the page do naturally. We’re supposed to feel the music. To imagine the entire poster pulsing to the beat like when you put sand on a speaker and watch it jump to the rhythm. It’s a gorgeous bit of sensory transference with sound being visualized as a warp speed burst flying past the central two men.
Drawn out

Tyler Rubenfeld goes literal with his hand-penciled poster for In the Mouth (limited, November 20). One man’s mustached lips open to hold the head of another man who subsequently holds the title in his. It’s like a Matryosha doll of faces. So much so that I’m surprised a third man (a smaller version of the first?) isn’t added to the chain rather than sat upon the second man’s shoulder.

The sheer lunacy is enough to turn heads, but the choice to go with black and white crosshatch amidst the usual slick photography of other posters guarantees it. Because even if you don’t notice the men from a distance due to the whole becoming a field of gray, the bright white of the title is unavoidable. The crisp edges render the letters into uncanny shapes so absent of color that they almost become mesmerizing tractor beams drawing us in closer.

Sam Smith’s Zi (limited, November 6) is drawn too, but with a computer rather than a pencil. Its outlined images look more like a map than a portrait as its vector line work overlap until its dual levels (black and red) merge to become one.

It’s a captivating image due to that flattening of perspective (despite the red image using perspective to mimic depth), but it’s a pitch-perfect calling card once you realize the thematic importance of this choice. Not to spoil anything, but Kogonada’s latest experimental feature plays with time in a way that allows its titular character to see her past and future selves in front of her depending on where and when she travels with in this city.

So, we’re talking about one drawing being projected on the other as much as a uniform coexistence between the two thanks to Smith’s wonderful decision to sometimes use both colors for a single line. They are simultaneously at odds and in concert. Dream and reality. Physical and illusion.

While Fourth Wall Studio’s poster for Birds of War (limited, November 4) isn’t fully illustrated like the previous two, its detailed drawings are exquisitely rendered to make you wonder if they should have left the two people below off the page completely.

That would be a mistake, though, considering this documentary is about them and the parallel lives they’ve lived over thirteen years of love, war, and exile. Their placement is therefore crucial to the whole because they become guardians of their two halves. The destruction in front of their camera lenses and the not quite symmetrical drawings above them of birds and bombs.

Two people. Two sides. One title treatment that merges the colors and motifs into a stunning block augmented by the red sun above and red tagline below. Black and white for detail. Red for color fields. Blue for a hopeful sky of possibility.
Boxed

While simple on its surface, Janie Stapleton’s Mouse (limited, November 6) packs a punch with that empty chair. This image is therefore as much about what we see as what we don’t. The weird depth of field reveals its probable Photoshop strings, but it too augments the fact that we’re supposed to be looking at both seats with equal importance. They pop out from the background—realistically or not.

I also just really like the balance of the text above and below the image frame. Everything at the top is shifted left. Everything at the bottom is shifted right. It’s a strong composition that gets to its point with purpose.

Jack Staniland’s (for CREATE) poster for Minotaur (limited, November 20) plays with its image box by repeating it six times for an effective conveyor belt effect that drags our vision through the page vertically from bottom to top. We’re stepping on rungs of a ladder as we rise from him to her (a new credit resting upon each separation) with a starkly brighter gap in-between showing a completely different scene of someone dragging a body outside. The latter is the perfect place to therefore situate the title on an island of its own.

You wouldn’t get that same motion had they just used the two images in full (one broken in half by the second). What would have been a stagnant triptych is now a subtly animated journey through emotional faces and uncertain fates.

Javier Jaén uses multiple image boxes for his Bitter Christmas (limited, November 13; wide, November 25) too. Rather than deconstruct and repeat an image, however, he turns this portrait into a collage of faces via multiple sets of eyes. It’s a stunning effect that causes us to imagine these six people all staring at the man whose image they cover. Think of the poster as a static representation of quick cuts around a dinner table at every guest revealing their current state of emotion. Or … are we seeing the different people who will look through that man’s eyes a la Being John Malkovich ?

That overload of potential information is why I think this is the best of the film’s three one-sheets. Jaén’s second optical illusion with a man’s silhouetted profile and a woman’s cropped portrait aligned off-center is a well-orchestrated visual, but it doesn’t have that same intrigue. Yes, you still get the notion of a blurred identity or focal point (the film tells two stories simultaneously), but it’s not nearly as evocative.

The same can be said for Andrew Bannister’s English-language iteration—although it’s a lot of fun, regardless. It uses color (blue and red) to denote the two narratives while also creating its own Matryoshka doll of cacti in cacti with a man’s head peeking out from inside too. The thorny foliage playing with the unusual use of “bitter” to describe a holiday generally synonymous with pleasure ties the whole together nicely.
